advances: A finite method for individual interval-fiber bodies. It gives the actual centroid path and a separate all-halfspace depth computation, without a uniform lower bound for their intersection.
author: PK-research-agent
proof:
Fix the mass on each interval. Its largest first moment is $u_i m_i-m_i^2/2$, obtained by taking the upper subinterval of length $m_i$. Indeed, subtract a competing dominated density from the upper interval indicator and integrate against the coordinate minus the fill threshold. The product is nonnegative pointwise and subtracting the threshold does not change its integral. Reversing orientation gives the lower interval and objective $-l_i m_i-m_i^2/2$ for the negative first moment. Every feasible allocation is realizable, and the finite box maximum is attained. Strict concavity gives uniqueness of its mass vector. The feasible densities form a convex set so the endpoints fill out the indicated interval. Its points belong to $K_j$ by convexity of $C$. Rescaling a dominated density by a factor in $(0,1)$ proves nesting. For $0<t\le w_j$ the two own-fiber fills give centroid coordinates $l_j+t/2$ and $u_j-t/2$, which together with containment in $K_j$ give the endpoint limit.

Each value $Q_v$ is concave by convex interpolation of feasible allocations and concavity of the objective. It is continuous at all masses: any sequence of maximizing allocations has convergent subsequences in the compact box, giving the upper limit, while interpolating a fixed optimizer with an allocation of higher or lower mass gives feasible nearby rows approaching it on the corresponding side. In particular $U(0)=V(0)=0$.

At a maximizing row, the gradient $v-m$ has nonpositive dot product with every feasible tangent direction. The directions have zero total and centered base moment, with nonnegative coordinates at empty entries and nonpositive coordinates at full entries. The polar of this finite polyhedral cone is the span of the two equality normals plus the cone of the active bound normals. This follows by separating any vector outside that closed polyhedral cone of normals, yielding a tangent direction with positive dot product. Hence for some finite $b,\nu$ the residual $v_i-m_i-b-\nu d_i$ is zero on free entries, nonpositive on empty entries and nonnegative on full entries. These are exactly the clamp equations, and they are sufficient by the exact objective difference $(v-m)\cdot(m'-m)-\lVert m'-m\rVert^2/2$: the equality-normal terms vanish and each bound term is nonpositive.

For a fixed pattern let $F$ be the full set. The two equality equations become
$$
\begin{aligned}
Sb+Z\nu&=\sum_{i\in A}v_i+\sum_{i\in F}w_i-t,\\
Zb+ZZ\nu&=\sum_{i\in A}d_i v_i+\sum_{i\in F}d_i w_i .
\end{aligned}
$$
If $|A|\ge2$, distinct $d_i$ give $S\cdot ZZ-Z^2>0$ and $ZZ>0$. Thus $b,\nu,m$ are affine in $t$, and the clamp conditions for this pattern are affine inequalities in $t$. Along the pattern only free masses vary. Their derivatives sum to one and have centered base moment zero, so differentiating the objective using $v_i-m_i=b+\nu d_i$ gives $Q_v'=b$. Differentiating the two displayed equations gives $b'=-1/(S-Z^2/ZZ)$. If only $j$ is free, its mass equals $t-\sum_{i\in F}w_i$ and $b=v_j-m_j$, so $b'=-1$. The base equation then requires the full indices to have zero centered moment. The empty/full inequalities give affine lower and upper bounds for $\nu$, and eliminating it amounts to comparing every lower bound with every upper bound. A sole free index other than $j$ has fixed mass by the base equation, and with no free index all masses are fixed.

The finitely many patterns cover the feasible mass interval. Each covers an interval or a point, and on its open interval the value is quadratic. Continuity supplies the boundary values. This gives a finite partition and absolute continuity including at zero. The upper-cap source takes $x\ge b_U+\nu_U d_i$ and the lower source takes $x\le-b_V-\nu_V d_i$. Their traces have the optimizing masses, so integrating the two value derivatives proves the stated average of the physical thresholds. The two source thresholds may come from different caps.

For rational data $T_j$ is rational by maximization over a bounded rational polytope. The pattern equations and affine inequalities give rational coefficients and rational breakpoints, and the common refinement for $U,V$ gives the stated form for $c_j$. A term $C_0/t$ cannot survive the finite limit at zero. Each piece has extrema at its endpoints and possibly at a positive critical mass $\sqrt{C_0/A}$ when $A\ne0$ and this root lies in the piece. A constant piece contributes its value. Continuity gives a single range interval, and testing the finite extrema and constant pieces determines whether either endpoint is attained at positive time.

To compute the original depth at $(j,y)$, first tighten a containing cap through that point. A downward nonvertical cap with slope $a$ has mass
$$
D(a,y)=\sum_i\operatorname{clamp}(y+ad_i-l_i,0,w_i).
$$
The complementary upward cap has mass $M-D(a,y)$ since each nonvertical cut has zero mixed boundary length. At fixed $y$, the slope breakpoints are $(l_i-y)/d_i$ and $(u_i-y)/d_i$ for $i\ne j$. The mass is affine between consecutive breakpoints and constant on the two unbounded intervals. Evaluate both orientations at all breakpoints and on both plateaus, and add the two pure-base masses, each of which includes the whole fiber at $j$. With no off-base breakpoint the slope mass is constant. Every evaluated mass is a rational piecewise affine function of $y$. The depth is their minimum. Its superlevel in $K_j$ is a closed interval or empty: for each orientation the infimum over slopes is monotone in $y$, in opposite directions, and both vertical budgets are constant. The endpoints of this interval at a rational level are computable by affine inequalities. Intersect with the computed positive-time range, excluding an endpoint when it is achieved only at $t=0$.
statement:
Let $C\subset\mathbb R^2$ be compact and convex, with integer-fiber length measure $\mu$. Its positive fibers are intervals $K_i=[l_i,u_i]$ of widths $w_i=u_i-l_i$ on the finite consecutive index set $P$. Fix $j\in P$, put $d_i=i-j$, $M=\sum_iw_i$, and let
$$
T_j=\max\left\{\sum_i m_i:0\le m_i\le w_i,\ \sum_i d_i m_i=0\right\}.
$$
For $0<t\le T_j$ let $B_j(t)$ be the interval of continuous centroids of dominated sources $0\le f\le1$ of mass $t$ and base centroid $j$. Let $c_j(t)$ be its midpoint, including the singleton convention. Write $Q_v(t)$ for the maximum of $\sum_i(v_i m_i-m_i^2/2)$ over the same box with centered base moment zero and $\sum_i m_i=t$. With $U=Q_u$ and $V=Q_{-l}$,
$$
 B_j(t)=[-V(t)/t,U(t)/t],\qquad c_j(t)=\frac{U(t)-V(t)}{2t}.
$$
Each optimizer is unique and has the form $m_i=\operatorname{clamp}(v_i-b-\nu d_i,0,w_i)$ for finite multipliers $b,\nu$, where $\operatorname{clamp}(x,0,w)=\min(w,\max(0,x))$. The intervals are nested in decreasing order as $t$ increases and $c_j(0)=(l_j+u_j)/2$ gives a continuous extension.

The functions $U,V$ are continuous finite piecewise quadratics on $[0,T_j]$. On any open interval of one fixed empty/free/full pattern with free set $A$ of at least two indices, set $S=|A|$, $Z=\sum_{i\in A}d_i$ and $ZZ=\sum_{i\in A}d_i^2$. Then $Q_v'=b$ and $Q_v''=-1/(S-Z^2/ZZ)$. If only $j$ is free on an open interval, then $Q_v'=b$ and $Q_v''=-1$. Denote the boundary values at base $j$ of the optimizing upper and lower caps by $b_+=b_U$ and $b_-=-b_V$, respectively. Away from finitely many transition masses they determine the path by
$$
c_j(t)=\frac{1}{2t}\int_0^t[b_+(s)+b_-(s)]\,ds.
$$
If all endpoints are rational, the path has form $At+B+C_0/t$ on finitely many rational mass intervals with rational coefficients, with $C_0=0$ on the first interval. Its range has rational or quadratic-algebraic endpoints with decidable endpoint inclusion. At any rational raw mixed-depth level, one can decide exactly whether a positive-time path point reaches that level in the original measure, using all closed halfspace orientations.
title: Exact varying-mass interval moment-centroid paths and depth intersections
